overview.body:
**Hati** ​(*hati*) — ‌Moon-Chaser, ‌Chaos · ​The ​hater — ​belongs to ​the ​Norse tradition, ‌where ​it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain ‌"Moon-Chaser, Chaos". ​The ‌name means ​"The hater"[^1].

​Hati ​Hróðvitnisson is ​the ​wolf who ‌runs ​before the ‌sun ​and after ‌the ​moon: son ‌of the ​fame-wolf ‌Fenrir, bred ​in ​the Ironwood, ‌and ‌fated to ‌seize ​Máni out ​of ‌the sky ​— the ​chase ‌on which ​the ​Edda hangs ‌its ​explanation of ‌the ​darkened moon ​and ​one of ​the certainties ‌of ‌Ragnarǫk.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores ‌the name ​as ​**Hati** and ‌serves ‌its temple ‌at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/hati/). ​The restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent ​form — ​a ​description computed ‌from ​the displayed ​form ​itself. The ‌plain ​ASCII form ​*hati* survives ​as ‌a modern ​convenience ‌imposed by ​the ‌early domain-name ​system; ‌the restoration, ‌not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form ​the project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of the ‌name is **/ˈhɑ.ti/** ‌— Old Norse ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- **H-** — ​Voiceless glottal ​fricative [h], as ​in English 'hat'; ‌Old Norse initial ​h is fully ​sounded.
- **-a-** — ‌Short open back ​unrounded [ɑ], held ‌brief — Old ​Norse short a, ‌not the long ​á.
- **-ti** — ​Voiceless dental stop ​[t] and ​short front [i]; ​the second syllable ‌is unstressed and ​clipped, as in ‌modern Icelandic.

For ​the modern speaker, ‌the closest approximation ​is: 'HAH-tih' — ‌two short syllables, ​stress on the ‌first; the vowels ​are short ​and plain, with ‌no diphthong and ‌no final nominative ‌-r, for the ​name ends in ​a stem vowel, ‌not an ending.

​Kindred and historical ​forms of the ‌name:

- **Old Norse** ​— Hati Hróðvitnisson, ​'Hati, son of ‌Hróðvitnir' — ​the fame-wolf's son ‌of Grímnismál and ​Gylfaginning.
- **Common noun** ​— hati, 'hater, ​enemy' — the ​ordinary Old Norse ‌agent noun, from ‌the verb hata, ​'to hate'.
- **English ‌cognate** — hate ​— the verb ​hata and English ‌hate descend ‌from the same ‌Proto-Germanic word, *hatōjan-.
- ‌**Modern Icelandic** — ​Hati, unchanged in ‌spelling since the ​medieval manuscripts.

Hati ​is a plain ​restoration by the ‌mechanical rule: the ​normalized Old Norse ​form is already ​plain ASCII ‌— there is ​no diacritic and ​no distinctive letter ​for the ASCII ‌alphabet to lose. ​Unlike most Old ‌Norse masculine theonyms ​it carries no ‌nominative -r, since ​the name is ‌the agent noun ‌hati ('the hater') ​with a ​weak-declension stem vowel. ​The name's transparency ​is its whole ‌story: the wolf ‌is called, simply, ​'the Hater'.

original-script.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved in ‌Younger ​Futhark as ​**ᚼᛅᛏᛁ**.[^1]

​The scholarly ​transliteration is ​*hati*.

‌The rendering ​proceeds step ​by ‌step:

- ᚼ ​(hagall) ‌writes /h/
- ​ᛅ (ár) ‌writes ​/a/, /á/ ​and /æ/
- ​ᛏ ​(Týr) writes ​both ‌/t/ and ​/d/
- The ‌spelling ​hati is ‌a normalized ​phonetic ‌reconstruction; Younger ​Futhark ‌does not ​distinguish voiced/voiceless ​stops ‌or separate ‌short and ‌long ​vowels

The ​normalized ‌Old Norse ​form is ​**Hati** ‌— already ​plain ASCII, ​with ‌no diacritic ​or ‌distinctive letter ​for the ​restoration ​to recover; ​in the ‌Younger ‌Futhark the ​name ‌would have ​been carved ​ᚼᛅᛏᛁ ‌(h-a-t-i, four ‌runes with ‌no ‌ambiguity). Because ​the ‌name is ​pure ASCII, ​its ​domain was ‌registered long ​ago ​in the ​ordinary ‌way: **hati.com ​is held ​by ​a third ‌party outside ​the ‌PuniCodex collection ​and ‌is watched ​for release** ‌— ‌no form ​of the ​name ​is currently ​owned, ‌and this ‌temple claims ​none.

domains.body:
Hati ​Hróðvitnisson is ‌the wolf ‌who runs ​before ​the sun ​and after ​the moon: ​son ‌of the ​fame-wolf Fenrir, ​bred in ‌the ​Ironwood, and ‌fated to ​seize Máni ‌out ​of the ​sky — ​the chase ​on ​which the ‌Edda hangs ​its explanation ‌of ​the darkened ‌moon and ​one of ‌the ​certainties of ‌Ragnarǫk.[^1]

### The ​Chase

Grímnismál's ​picture: ‌Hati runs ‌before the ‌bright bride ​of ​heaven — ‌ahead of ​the sun, ​at ‌the heels ​of the ​moon that ‌flees ​before her.

### ‌Hróðvitnir's Son

​The patronymic ​names ​his father: ​Hróðvitnir, 'fame-wolf', ‌a heiti ‌of ​Fenrir himself ‌— the ​apocalyptic kennel's ​own ‌lineage.

### Járnviðr, ‌the Ironwood

‌Völuspá's forest ‌east ​of the ‌world, where ​the old ​giantess ​breeds Fenrir's ‌brood — ​and from ​them ​all comes ‌the one ​who takes ​the ​moon.

### The ‌Seized Moon

​The catch ‌Snorri ​says must ‌come: the ​moon swallowed, ‌the ‌sky spattered ​with blood, ​and the ​light ​of the ‌world going ‌out at ​Ragnarǫk.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 12 (Skǫll and Hati; Mánagarmr) and 51 (Ragnarǫk); Skáldskaparmál þulur (wolf-heiti).

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Hati ​concentrates in ​a ​small ​set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each ​a ‌compressed ​statement about ‌the ​name:[^1]

- ​**The ​running ​wolf** ​— ‌Pursuit ​without ‌rest: the ​sky ‌itself ​read ‌as ​a ‌hunt ​that ​has ‌never ‌once paused
- ‌**The ​fleeing ​moon** ‌— ​Máni's ​course ‌as ​flight ​— ‌the measured ​path ‌of ​the ​heavens ​reinterpreted ​as ‌terror
- ‌**Járnviðr, ​the ‌Ironwood** — ​The ​eastern ‌forest ‌where ‌the ‌wolf-brood ​is ‌bred: ​chaos ​with an ​address, ‌growing ​older ​by ​the ‌year
- ​**The ​darkened ​sky** — ‌Völuspá's ​'the ‌sunshine ​turns ‌black' ​— ‌the ‌eclipse ​and ​the world's ​ending ​written ‌in ‌one ​image

mythology.body:
Hati's mythology is a ​single image carried by a handful of ‌verses: a wolf, a moon, and ‌a chase that ends only with the ​world. The Poetic Edda names him once, ​Snorri gives him his quarry and his ​ending, and Völuspá's seeress supplies the brood ​he springs from.[^1]

### The Pair Before ​Heaven (Grímnismál 39)

The name's one poetic ‌attestation comes in Óðinn's great catalogue of ​the cosmos in Grímnismál, where the disguised ​god enumerates the heavens for the torture-bound ‌Geirrøðr: 'Skǫll is the name of ​the wolf who follows the bright-faced god ‌to the sheltering wood; but the other ​is Hati, Hróðvitnir's son, who runs before ‌the bright bride of heaven.' The ​bright bride of heaven is the sun; ​the wolf who runs before her is ​on the heels of the moon, which ​travels ahead of her. In four lines ​the Edda converts the machinery of ‌the sky into a hunt: what astronomy ​calls a course, the poem calls a ‌chase.[^2]

### Skǫll After the Sun, Hati After ​the Moon (Gylfaginning 12)

Snorri systematizes ‌the verse. When Gangleri asks why the ​sun hurries so — 'she speeds as ‌if she were afraid' — High One ​answers that she has good cause: 'the ‌one who seeks her is right ​behind her, and she has no other ​way out than to run.' Two wolves ‌do the work of the heavens: Skǫll ‌chases the sun and will catch her, ‌and 'the other wolf is called ​Hati Hróðvitnisson; he runs in front of ​her and wants to catch the moon ‌— and that is what will happen.' ​Snorri's gloss fixes the reading the ​poem left compressed, and with it the ‌moon's doom is put on the schedule ​of things foretold.

### Mánagarmr, the Moon-Hound (Gylfaginning ​12)

In the same chapter Snorri names ‌the mightiest of the wolf-brood: Mánagarmr, ​'moon-hound' — 'he will be filled with ‌the flesh of all who die, and ​he will swallow the moon and spatter ​the sky and all the air with ​blood; from this the sun will ​lose its brightness.' Whether Mánagarmr is Hati ‌under a second name or a third ‌wolf beside the pair, the manuscripts and ​the handbooks leave open; Simek and ‌Lindow record the identification as probable but ​unprovable. What is certain is the image: ​the moon taken, and the blood of ‌the swallowed light staining heaven.

### The Brood ‌of the Ironwood (Völuspá 39-40)

Völuspá's ‌seeress supplies the kennel. 'In the east ‌sat the old one in the Ironwood ​and bred there Fenrir's brood; from all ‌of them comes one in particular, a ​snatcher of the moon in a ​troll's skin. He gorges on the life ​of doomed men, reddens the gods' dwellings ‌with red blood; the sunshine turns black ​in the summers after, and all ​weathers run hostile.' The poem names no ​name — but the tungls tjúgari, the ‌'snatcher of the moon', is the role ​Grímnismál and Snorri assign to Hati, and ​the handbooks read the figures together: ​the Ironwood breeds the chase, and the ‌chase ends the world.

### The Catch at ​Ragnarǫk (Gylfaginning 51 · Völuspá)

The ending ‌is shared by every witness. When ​Ragnarǫk comes, the wolves' running stops: Skǫll ‌takes the sun, Hati takes the moon, ​Fenrir himself swallows Óðinn, and 'the sun ‌turns black, earth sinks into the sea, ‌the bright stars vanish from the ​sky.' The Edda's cosmology is built so ​that the nightly order of the heavens ​is only an interval — the long ​meanwhile between the start of the chase ‌and its foreknown end. Hati never ‌fails of his quarry; he simply has ​not caught it yet.

syncretism.body:
Hati has ​no cult, ‌no continental ‌cognate, and ​no existence ​outside the ​Eddic record: ​he belongs ​to the North's ‌own eschatological ​machinery. Scholars ​since the ‌nineteenth century ​have noted ‌that the ​doubling of ‌the apocalyptic wolf ​— one ​chasing the ​sun, one ​the moon ​— is ‌probably a ​secondary systematization ‌of the older ​single figure, ‌the bound ​Fenrir who ‌breaks loose ​at the ‌world's end; ​Simek and ​Lindow treat Skǫll ‌and Hati ‌as elaborations ‌within the ​Fenrir-complex rather ​than independent ‌tradition. What ​the pair ​does uniquely well ‌is etiology: ​the chase ​gives the ‌sky a ​reason for ‌its haste, ​and the ​wolf drawing near ​gives the ​North its ‌explanation of ‌the eclipse ​— when ‌the pursuer ​closes, the ​moon darkens. The ‌devouring-monster account ‌of eclipses ‌is a ‌comparative commonplace ​across cultures; ‌the Norse ​version is ​distinctive for giving ​its monsters ‌names, a ​pedigree, and ​a date.[^1]

​Kindred figures ‌in the ​PuniCodex cross-tradition ​index include [[angrboda|Angrboða]] ​(chaos / ‌primordial / ​world serpent), ‌[[apep|ꜥꜣpp]] (chaos ​/ primordial ‌/ world ​serpent), [[artemis|Ártemis]] ‌(moon / lunar), ‌[[change|Chángé]] (moon ​/ lunar), ​[[chaos|Cháos]] (chaos ​/ primordial ​/ world ‌serpent), and ‌[[hekate|Hekátē]] (moon ​/ lunar).

cultural-legacy.body: Hati's ​afterlife ‌is the ‌eclipse-wolf's: ​wherever ​the ​Ragnarǫk story ​is ​retold, ‌the ​pair Skǫll ​and ‌Hati ​run in ‌the ​sky ‌above ​it. Victorian ​and ​later ​handbooks ​of Norse ‌myth ​made ‌the ​chase a ‌set-piece ​of ‌cosmological ​explanation — ‌the ​sky's ​motions ‌as a ‌hunt, ‌the ​eclipse as ​the ‌moment ​the ​wolf gains ‌— ​and ​modern ‌retellings, novels, ​and ‌games ​keep ​the two ​wolves ​as ‌Ragnarǫk's ‌outriders. In ​scholarship ‌the ​name is ​the ‌standing ‌example ‌of the ‌Edda's ​transparent ‌theonymy: ​a god-figure ​called, ​without ‌ornament, ​'the Hater'. ​The ​name ‌never ​entered the ​living ​name-pool ‌as ​Baldr's did; ‌it ​survives ‌where it ​was ‌born, ‌in ​the poetry, ​doing ​the ​one ‌job it ‌was ​given.[^1]

archaeology.body: Hati ​is a ‌wholly textual ‌figure: ​no runestone ​names him, ​no ​votive deposit ​invokes him, ‌and ​no image ​can be ‌securely ​assigned to ‌him. Wolf ​iconography ‌is plentiful ​in the ​Viking-Age ​record — ​the wolf-rider ​and ‌great-wolf scenes ​on ‌the Gotland ​picture stones ‌have ​long been ‌argued over, ​and ‌Hyrrokkin's wolf-mount ​at Baldr's ​funeral ‌was carved ‌in Óláfr ‌pái's ​hall (Húsdrápa, ​c. 983) ‌— ​but no ​carving carries ‌an ​inscription that ​ties a ‌wolf ​to the ‌moon-chase. The ​name's ​witnesses are ​the manuscripts: ​Grímnismál ‌in the ‌Codex Regius ​(c. ‌1270) and ​AM 748 ​I ‌4to, Völuspá ‌in the ‌Codex ‌Regius and ​Hauksbók, and ‌Gylfaginning ​in the ​Codex Regius ​of ‌the Prose ​Edda ​and its ​sister codices ‌(Codex ​Wormianus, Codex ​Upsaliensis), all ​recording ‌material centuries ​older. The ‌þulur ​of Skáldskaparmál ‌preserve Hati ​and ‌Hróðvitnir among ‌the poetic ​heiti ​for 'wolf' ​— the ​tradition's ‌own file ‌of the ​name.[^1]

meditation.body: Hati ​is the ‌Edda's ‌most economical ​idea: take ​the ​verb 'to ​hate', ​give it ‌legs, ​and set ​it ‌running after ​the light. ‌There ​is no ‌malice-scene, ​no dialogue, ​no ​character beyond ​the ​name — ‌only pursuit. ​And ‌that is ​the ‌point. The ​Norse ‌imagination looked ​at ‌the most ​orderly thing ​in ‌the world, ‌the ‌clockwork of ​sun ​and moon, ‌and ​read it ​as flight: ‌the ​lights hurry ​because ‌something hates ​them ‌and is ​coming. ​Time itself ​becomes the ​distance ‌still left ‌between ​the wolf ‌and ​the moon ​— ‌every night ‌the moon ‌escapes ‌is a ​night ‌the world ​continues. ​Hati asks ​the ‌uncomfortable question ​the whole ​Ragnarǫk ​cycle asks: ‌how ​do you ​keep ​the light ‌moving, ​knowing exactly ‌what follows ​it? ‌The Edda's ​answer ‌is the ‌one ​it gives ​everywhere. ​You keep ​running. The ‌chase ‌is the ​world.[^1]
